lessons.title: Jesus as Messiah, Son of Man and the Baptism

before.exam_tip_html: For “Explain two…” questions, make sure each explanation is developed — don’t just name the title or passage. For example, don’t just say “Jesus is called Son of Man” — explain what it meant and why it mattered. For the 5-mark question, remember the fifth mark depends on a named source: a book and passage (e.g. “In Daniel 7:13…” or “In Isaiah 53…”). For 12-mark Discuss questions, develop both sides fully — a common weakness is spending three paragraphs on the Christian view and one sentence on the Humanist or atheist response. SPaG marks are available on selected 12-mark questions — spell ‘Messiah’, ‘omnipotence’ and ‘apocalyptic’ correctly and use them precisely.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Old Testament expectations of the Messiah at the time of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete points, e.g.:
• Many expected a warrior king in the tradition of David who would defeat Rome by force.
• Some hoped for a priestly figure who would restore pure worship in the Temple.
• Others anticipated a prophetic voice, like Elijah, calling the nation to repentance.
• Isaiah 53 describes a suffering servant — though this interpretation was not widely held before Jesus.

practice_questions.text: Describe the events of the baptism of Jesus as recorded in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points, e.g.:
• Jesus came from Galilee to be baptised by John in the River Jordan.
• As Jesus came up from the water, the heavens were 'torn open' and the Holy Spirit descended on him like a dove.
• A voice from heaven declared: 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the baptism of Jesus is important for Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per reason: one for a basic point, two for a developed explanation.
• The baptism established Jesus's identity as the Son of God, confirmed by the Father's voice — this gives Christians confidence that Jesus truly was divine, supporting the doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation.
• The baptism models the Christian sacrament of baptism — since Jesus submitted to baptism himself, most denominations see it as the rite of initiation into the Church, marking the beginning of a Christian's life of faith.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the title 'Son of Man' helps Christians understand who Jesus is.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point (one for point, one for development), plus one mark for a named source:
• 'Son of Man' connects Jesus to Daniel 7:13, where a heavenly figure is given 'dominion and glory and a kingdom' by God — this shows Jesus as a cosmic figure with divine authority, not just a human teacher.
• Jesus also uses 'Son of Man' when predicting his own suffering and death, showing that the path to glory runs through sacrifice — this shapes Christian understanding of the cross as necessary and purposeful.
The fifth mark requires citing Daniel 7:13 (or Isaiah 53) as a named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Mark's Gospel presents Jesus mainly as a suffering servant rather than a triumphant Messiah.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; conclusion weighs the evidence and reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present.
Developing (4-6): One side more developed; few or no named sources; conclusion is descriptive.
Emerging (1-3): One-sided or very brief; minimal development.

Arguments in support: Isaiah 53 describes a 'suffering servant' — wounded for others' transgressions — which Christians apply to Jesus. The Son of Man title is used both for glory (Daniel 7:13) and for suffering/death. Mark's Gospel consistently shows the disciples failing to understand a Messiah who must suffer. The passion narrative is central to Mark's structure.
Arguments against: The baptism (Mark 1:9-11) presents a triumphant divine commissioning — the Father speaks, the Spirit descends. The Daniel 7:13 'Son of Man' is a figure of cosmic power and eternal kingship. The transfiguration (Mark 9:1-10) shows Jesus's divine glory. Mark ends with an empty tomb — resurrection implies triumph.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• John preached in the desert, calling people to repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of sins.
• He pointed forward to a greater figure coming after him — someone so superior that John was not worthy to untie his sandals.
• He baptised Jesus in the River Jordan, at which point the Spirit descended and God identified Jesus as his Son.

before.exam_tip_html: For “Outline three” questions on miracles, give three genuinely separate points — don’t describe the same miracle from three angles. For the 5-mark question, identify a specific passage (e.g. “In Mark 4:35–41…”) as your source of authority — the passage reference earns the fifth mark automatically. For 12-mark Discuss questions on miracles, the Humanist/atheist perspective is the ‘other side’ that needs genuine development — one sentence is not enough. A good response explains their argument (natural-law regularity, scientific explanation, metaphorical reading) before offering the Christian counter-response. SPaG is tested on selected 12-mark questions: spell ‘Humanist’ with a capital H, and use ‘miraculous’ and ‘divine’ precisely.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen in Mark's account of the calming of the storm (Mark 4:35-41).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete accurate point:
• A violent squall arose while Jesus and the disciples were crossing the Sea of Galilee.
• Jesus, who was asleep, woke up and commanded the wind and waves to be still — they obeyed immediately.
• The disciples were terrified and asked 'Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey him!'

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens in Mark's account of the healing of Legion (Mark 5:1-20).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jesus met a man in the Gerasene region possessed by many demons who called themselves 'Legion'.
• Jesus commanded the demons out; they entered a herd of pigs that rushed into the lake and drowned.
• Afterwards the man was found sitting, clothed and in his right mind; the townspeople begged Jesus to leave.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the feeding of the five thousand (Mark 6:32-44) is important for Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per reason:
• The miracle shows Jesus's compassion for physical human need — he saw the crowd as 'sheep without a shepherd' and fed them, inspiring Christians to work for food justice and social care today.
• The actions of taking, blessing, breaking and giving bread echo the Last Supper and the Eucharist — this miracle points forward to the central Christian act of worship, giving it deep sacramental significance.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:21-43) shows who Jesus is.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point (one for the point, one for development), plus one mark for a named source:
• The miracle shows Jesus has power over death — he arrives after the girl has died, dismisses the mourners who laugh at him, and restores her to life with the command 'Talitha koum' (meaning 'Little girl, get up'), suggesting divine authority beyond ordinary human power.
• The miracle shows Jesus's compassion and personal care — he takes her hand, raises her gently, and tells her family to give her something to eat, showing a God who cares for individuals and their ordinary needs.
The fifth mark requires citing Mark 5:21-43 (or the Aramaic phrase 'Talitha koum' from the passage) as the source.

practice_questions.text:
'The miracles in Mark's Gospel prove that Jesus was the Son of God.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few named sources.
Emerging (1-3): One-sided, minimal.

In support: The miracles show power over nature (storm, water), supply (feeding), evil (Legion) and death (Jairus's daughter) — all attributed in Jewish thought to God alone. The disciples' question 'Who is this?' implies the miracles are pointing to a divine identity. The feeding echoes Elijah and Moses, placing Jesus in the tradition of God's prophets.
Against: Humanists argue miracles can be scientifically explained or are literary/symbolic. Atheists argue the texts were written decades after Jesus and reflect the beliefs of the early Church rather than historical events. Even within Christianity, not all believers interpret the miracles as literal — some read them as powerful symbols of God's care and power rather than physical interventions.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the miracles in Mark's Gospel show Jesus's compassion.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• In the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus has compassion on the crowd 'because they were like sheep without a shepherd' (Mark 6:34) and provides for their physical hunger.
• In the healing of Legion (Mark 5:1-20), Jesus restores a deeply disturbed man who is living in isolation and pain — the result is dignity: 'sitting, clothed and in his right mind'.
• In the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:21-43), Jesus responds immediately to a father's grief and takes the girl's hand gently, telling her family to give her something to eat.

lessons.title: Peter's Confession, the Transfiguration and Conflicts of Jesus

before.exam_tip_html: For questions on Peter’s confession, always include what Jesus said next — the passion prediction and the rebuke of Peter. This shows your understanding of the messianic secret and why Peter’s confession was partial. For the Transfiguration question, mention both Moses and Elias by name and explain what each represents (Law and Prophets) — examiners look for this detail. For 5-mark questions on Jesus’s conflicts, name the specific passage (e.g. “In Mark 2:1–12, Jesus healed a paralysed man and claimed to forgive his sins…”) to earn the source mark. SPaG note: ‘Transfiguration’ is a technical theological term — spell it accurately. Use ‘messianic secret’ and ‘Elias’ (Edexcel’s transliteration) correctly.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen during the Transfiguration of Jesus in Mark's Gospel (Mark 9:1-10).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Jesus's clothes became 'dazzling white, whiter than anyone in the world could bleach them.'
• Moses and Elias appeared and talked with Jesus.
• A voice from a cloud declared: 'This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!'

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens when Jesus and his disciples arrive at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27-33).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jesus asked the disciples who people said he was — they reported various views (John the Baptist, Elijah, a prophet).
• Peter declared: 'You are the Messiah.'
• Jesus predicted his own suffering and death; when Peter rebuked him, Jesus said 'Get behind me, Satan!'

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the conflicts of Jesus with the authorities in Mark's Gospel show what Jesus believed about himself.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• When Jesus healed the paralysed man (Mark 2:1-12) he first forgave his sins, claiming a power that belongs to God alone — the scribes were correct that 'only God can forgive sins', but Jesus's claim was that as Son of Man he possessed this divine authority.
• In the Sabbath controversies (Mark 2:23-3:6), Jesus called himself 'Lord of the Sabbath' — the Sabbath was established by God in the Torah, so claiming lordship over it was a claim to divine authority over the Law itself.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the cleansing of the Temple (Mark 11:15-18) is important in Mark's Gospel.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one mark for a named source:
• The Temple cleansing shows Jesus acting as a prophetic voice against corruption — by quoting Isaiah 56:7 ('My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations'), Jesus uses scripture to justify his action and claim that the Temple has become corrupted.
• The cleansing triggers the authorities' plot to kill Jesus — Mark 11:18 says 'the chief priests and teachers of the law began looking for a way to kill him', making it the moment that sets the passion narrative in motion.
The fifth mark requires citing Isaiah 56:7 or Jeremiah 7:11 as a named scriptural source Jesus quotes.

practice_questions.text:
'The messianic secret in Mark's Gospel shows that Jesus did not want to be recognised as the Messiah.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources and scholars; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Throughout Mark, Jesus commands silence after healings and miracles (e.g. after Jairus's daughter, after the healing of the leper). William Wrede argued the secrecy was Mark's theological invention to explain why Jesus was not widely recognised. Peter's well-meaning but misguided confession shows how dangerous the Messiah label was — it led immediately to misunderstanding about suffering.
Against: Jesus did not always silence people (the Gerasene demoniac was told to go and tell his family what God had done — Mark 5:19). The pattern may reflect Jesus's desire to control the terms of his mission rather than complete secrecy. At Peter's confession Jesus is not silent — he corrects, he predicts, he teaches. The Transfiguration suggests disclosure is coming but must wait until 'after the Son of Man has risen from the dead' (Mark 9:9).

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why the appearance of Moses and Elias at the Transfiguration is significant.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Moses represents the Law (Torah) — his presence shows Jesus is connected to and fulfils the Jewish Law.
• Elias (Elijah) represents the Prophets — in Jewish tradition, Elijah was expected to return before the Messiah came.
• Together, Moses and Elias signify that Jesus is the fulfillment of the whole of the Hebrew scriptures — Law and Prophets alike point to him.

flashcard_questions.q: Where was Peter's confession, and what did he say?

flashcard_questions.a: 'Get behind me, Satan! You do not have in mind the concerns of God, but merely human concerns.'
flashcard_questions.q: What did Jesus say to Peter immediately after the confession?

flashcard_questions.a: Jesus's repeated commands to keep his identity secret; identified by scholar William Wrede in 1901.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the messianic secret in Mark's Gospel?
What passage records the Transfiguration in Mark?

flashcard_questions.a: Moses (representing the Law) and Elias (representing the Prophets).
flashcard_questions.q: Who appeared with Jesus at the Transfiguration?

flashcard_questions.a: 'This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!'
flashcard_questions.q: What did the voice from the cloud say at the Transfiguration?

flashcard_questions.a: 'The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.'
flashcard_questions.q: What was Jesus's claim in Mark 2:28?

flashcard_questions.a: Isaiah 56:7 ('house of prayer for all nations') and Jeremiah 7:11 ('den of robbers').
flashcard_questions.q: What two Old Testament passages did Jesus quote when cleansing the Temple?

flashcard_questions.a: Edexcel's archaic transliteration of Elijah — use 'Elias' in answers, not 'Elijah', when citing spec passages.
flashcard_questions.q: What is 'Elias' and why does it matter for this spec?

flashcard_questions.a: The chief priests and scribes began plotting to kill him (Mark 11:18).
flashcard_questions.q: What was the immediate result of the Temple cleansing for Jesus?

flashcard_questions.a: Forgive sins — they accused Jesus of blasphemy.
flashcard_questions.q: In the healing of the paralysed man, what did the scribes say that only God could do?

lessons.title: The Last Days of Jesus and the Passion

before.content_html:
The Last Supper (Mark 14:12–31)

On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jesus instructs two of his disciples to prepare the Passover meal. The evening meal that follows (Mark 14:12–31) becomes one of the most theologically significant events in the whole New Testament. While they are eating, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it to his disciples saying: “Take it; this is my body.” He then takes a cup, gives thanks and shares it, saying: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”

This is the institution of what Christians call the Eucharist. The language of “covenant” and blood echoes Exodus 24, where Moses sprinkled blood on the people to seal the covenant at Sinai. Jesus reframes the Passover — a celebration of liberation from Egypt — as a new covenant sealed with his own death. This passage is the scriptural foundation for Christian sacramental practice across all denominations.

Also in this passage, Jesus predicts that one of the Twelve will betray him. He predicts that all of them will “fall away” and specifically that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice. These predictions set the stage for the passion narrative that follows.

Key Fact

The Last Supper passage is Mark 14:12–31. The central actions are: Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says “This is my body.” He takes the cup, gives thanks, shares it, and says “This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many.” This is the basis for the Eucharist celebrated in churches worldwide.

Gethsemane (Mark 14:32–42)

After the meal, Jesus takes his disciples to the garden of Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:32–42). He takes Peter, James and John deeper into the garden and tells them: “My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” He falls to the ground and prays: “Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.”

He returns to find the disciples asleep. He wakes them, returns to pray, comes back again and finds them sleeping again. A third time the same. This threefold pattern (like Peter’s threefold denial) is a literary device in Mark emphasising the disciples’ failure at the crucial moment. Jesus’s prayer — especially the address “Abba” (an intimate Aramaic term for Father) — shows a real human struggle with the prospect of death, while the submission “yet not what I will, but what you will” models obedient trust.

The Betrayal and Arrest (Mark 14:43–52)

While Jesus is still speaking, Judas Iscariot arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests. Judas identifies Jesus with a kiss — the customary greeting between a student and his rabbi, now perverted into a signal for arrest. One of the bystanders draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Jesus challenges his arresting party: “Am I leading a rebellion, that you have come out with swords and clubs to capture me? Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest me.”

Mark then adds a striking detail found only in his Gospel: a young man following Jesus, wearing nothing but a linen garment, is seized. He flees naked, leaving his garment behind. Scholars debate whether this is the author’s subtle self-insertion into the story, a symbolic detail (nakedness as shame), or simply an eyewitness memory included for vividness.

The Trials (Mark 14:53–65; 15:1–15)

Jesus faces two separate trials. In Mark 14:53–65, he is brought before the High Priest and the Sanhedrin. Witnesses are produced but their testimony does not agree. Finally the High Priest asks directly: “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?” Jesus answers: “I am.” He adds that they will see “the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Mighty One and coming on the clouds of heaven.” The High Priest tears his clothes and declares blasphemy. Jesus is condemned to death.

In Mark 15:1–15, Jesus is brought before Pilate. Pilate asks: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus replies: “You have said so.” He gives no further answer, to Pilate’s amazement. Pilate offers to release a prisoner as was his custom at the festival — but the crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, call for Barabbas. Pilate asks what to do with Jesus; they shout “Crucify him!” Pilate, “wishing to satisfy the crowd,” hands Jesus over to be crucified.

In first-century Judaea, the Sanhedrin (Jewish ruling council) had authority over religious law but could not carry out the death penalty without Roman authorisation. This is why Jesus faces two trials: the Sanhedrin condemns him for blasphemy (Mark 14:53–65), and Pilate then must authorise the crucifixion (Mark 15:1–15). The Jewish authorities wanted Jesus dead but needed Rome to do it. This two-stage legal process is consistent with what historians know about Roman provincial governance.

Each trial has a different focus. The High Priest’s trial revolves around Jesus’s identity: “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?” Pilate’s trial revolves around political threat: “Are you the king of the Jews?” The Sanhedrin charge is blasphemy; the Roman charge must be sedition against Caesar. Mark shows how the same claim — that Jesus is the Christ — is processed differently by Jewish religious law and Roman political law.

The Passion and Crucifixion (Mark 15:21–39)

Jesus is crucified at a place called Golgotha (“the place of the skull”) at nine in the morning. Mark notes that Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. At midday, darkness covers the land for three hours. At three in the afternoon, Jesus cries out in Aramaic: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” — which Mark translates as “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” This is the opening line of Psalm 22, a psalm that moves from abandonment to vindication.

Jesus utters a loud cry and breathes his last. At that moment, the curtain of the Temple is “torn in two from top to bottom” — a symbol that the barrier between God and humanity has been removed. Immediately the Roman centurion standing opposite Jesus says: “Surely this man was the Son of God!” In Mark’s Gospel, this is the first time a human being — not a demon — correctly identifies Jesus with this title while he is alive. And it is a Roman soldier, a Gentile outsider, who says it.

Key Fact

The centurion’s confession at the cross — “Surely this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39) — is the climax of Mark’s narrative on Jesus’s identity. It is spoken by a Gentile Roman soldier at the moment of death, not triumph. This reflects Mark’s whole theology: Jesus’s divine identity is revealed in and through the cross, not despite it.

The Resurrection: The Empty Tomb (Mark 16:1–8)

On the first day of the week, three women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome — come to the tomb to anoint the body. They find the stone already rolled away and a young man in white inside who tells them: “He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’”

Mark’s Gospel ends at this point (16:8): “Trembling and bewildered, the women went out and fled from the tomb. They said nothing to anyone, because they were afraid.” This is the authentic ending of Mark. The abruptness is deliberate — the reader is left with the empty tomb, the proclamation, and the challenge to believe and follow. There is no appearance of the risen Jesus in the genuine Markan text. This ending has troubled Christians across the centuries, which is why later scribes added a “longer ending” (Mark 16:9–20) that most scholars consider a later addition, not part of the original Gospel.

The ending at 16:8 — with the women fleeing in fear — is theologically rich rather than incomplete. Mark has shown disciples who repeatedly fail, misunderstand and abandon Jesus. The women at the tomb are the disciples’ last chance, and they too fail to deliver the message. Yet the risen Jesus has gone ahead to Galilee. The open ending invites the reader to become the one who does go to Galilee, who does tell the disciples, who does follow. Some scholars argue Mark ended abruptly because the original last page of the scroll was lost; others argue the ending is deliberate.

Christians who find the ending abrupt are reassured by the other Gospels (Matthew, Luke and John), which all record resurrection appearances. But for students of Mark specifically, the challenge of the spec is to understand Mark 16:1–8 on its own terms — the empty tomb, the proclamation, and the challenge to respond in faith. This is the authentic Markan witness to the resurrection.
before.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers the highest-density section of Mark — many passages and multiple events. For “Outline three” questions, practise picking three genuinely distinct points from one passage. For the 5-mark question, name the specific passage as your source (e.g. “In Mark 14:32–42, the Gethsemane prayer shows Jesus saying ‘not what I will, but what you will’…”). Never cite Mark 16:9–20 as part of Mark’s original ending — the spec specifies Mark 16:1–8. For 12-mark Discuss questions on the resurrection, compare Christian responses (empty tomb, eyewitness testimony in other Gospels) with non-religious views (disciples’ psychological experiences, later legend). SPaG: spell ‘Gethsemane’, ‘Eucharist’ and ‘Sanhedrin’ correctly — all are technical terms worth marks.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Jesus did and said at the Last Supper in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said 'Take it; this is my body.'
• He took a cup, gave thanks, shared it and said 'This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.'
• He predicted that one of the Twelve would betray him, and that Peter would deny him three times.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Jesus said and did in the Garden of Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jesus told his disciples 'My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death' and asked them to keep watch.
• He prayed: 'Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.'
• He returned three times to find the disciples sleeping rather than keeping watch.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the crucifixion narrative (Mark 15:21-39) shows who Jesus is.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Jesus's final cry — 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — quotes Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in abandonment but moves toward vindication; this shows him as the suffering servant of the scriptures whose death fulfils God's plan.
• The centurion's confession — 'Surely this man was the Son of God' — is the theological climax of Mark's Gospel; the first human to correctly identify Jesus during his lifetime is a Gentile Roman soldier, showing that the cross reveals Jesus's identity and that salvation is for all peoples.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the events of Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42) are important for Christians.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for a named source:
• Gethsemane shows Jesus's full humanity — he is 'overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death', demonstrating that the Incarnation was real and that Jesus faced death with genuine fear, which gives Christians comfort when facing their own suffering.
• Gethsemane models submission to God's will — 'not what I will, but what you will' (Mark 14:36) shows perfect obedient trust, which Christians see as the model for prayer and discipleship: bringing one's desires to God but ultimately trusting God's purpose.
The fifth mark requires citing Mark 14:32-42 (or the specific prayer 'Abba, Father... not what I will, but what you will') as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The empty tomb is the most important part of the passion narrative in Mark's Gospel.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Without the empty tomb (Mark 16:1-8), the passion narrative would end in failure. The young man's proclamation 'He has risen!' transforms the cross from defeat into victory. Christianity is founded on the resurrection claim; St Paul later wrote 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17). The empty tomb is the beginning of the disciples' mission.
Against: The Last Supper (Mark 14:12-31) is arguably the heart of the passion narrative — it gives theological meaning to the cross (new covenant, poured out for many) before the death happens. The centurion's confession (Mark 15:39) is the climax of Mark's theology on Jesus's identity. The crucifixion itself, not the empty tomb, is the act of salvation in Christian theology. Mark's Gospel focuses the reader on the cross more than on resurrection appearances.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happened at the tomb on the first day of the week (Mark 16:1-8).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Three women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome — came to the tomb to anoint Jesus's body.
• They found the stone rolled away and a young man in white inside who told them 'He has risen! He is not here.'
• The women fled from the tomb trembling and bewildered, and said nothing to anyone because they were afraid.

glossary_terms.definition: The Christian sacrament of bread and wine, also called Holy Communion or the Mass; instituted by Jesus at the Last Supper and celebrated in Christian worship ever since.
The garden on the Mount of Olives where Jesus prayed in anguish before his arrest; the name means 'oil press'.
The Jewish ruling council, also called the Sanhedrin; led by the High Priest, it had authority over religious law and could recommend the death penalty to the Romans.
The Roman governor of Judaea at the time of Jesus's crucifixion.
The suffering and death of Jesus, particularly the crucifixion; from the Latin 'passio' meaning suffering.
The resurrection claim that Jesus rose bodily from the dead.

lessons.title: Discipleship: The Call, the Cost and Living It Today

before.content_html:
The Call of the Disciples

Discipleship in Mark’s Gospel begins with a simple, urgent invitation. In Mark 1:14–20, Jesus walks beside the Sea of Galilee and calls Simon and Andrew, then James and John. Each time, the response is immediate: “Immediately they left their nets and followed him.” There is no lengthy deliberation, no negotiation. The disciples abandon their livelihoods on the spot. In Mark 2:13–17, Jesus calls Levi, a tax collector — a figure despised as a Roman collaborator — with the same two words: “Follow me.” Levi gets up and follows.

This pattern communicates something important about what Mark means by discipleship: it is a total reorientation of life, not a part-time commitment. Scholars note that in the ancient world, students usually chose their rabbi; here, Jesus chooses his disciples. This reversal is deliberate. The disciples did not graduate to follow Jesus — they were called, often from ordinary working lives, and they left everything in response.

In Mark 6:7–13, Jesus sends out the Twelve on a mission. He sends them “two by two” and instructs them to “take nothing for the journey except a staff — no bread, no bag, no money in their belts.” They are to travel light, depend on the hospitality of others, and preach repentance. This commissioning extends the model: discipleship is not just internal formation but active participation in Jesus’s mission.

The Parables of Discipleship

Two parables in Mark address what discipleship looks like in practice.

The Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:1–20) describes four kinds of soil: the path (no response), rocky ground (initial enthusiasm that withers), thorny ground (choked by wealth and worries), and good soil (bearing fruit). Jesus explains that the seed is “the word.” The parable is a sobering map of how differently people receive the invitation to follow Jesus, and it connects directly to the Kingdom of God — the disciples are called to be “good soil,” remaining receptive to God’s word even when life makes it difficult.

The Parable of the Tenants (Mark 12:1–12) is a allegory about Israel’s history of rejecting God’s messengers. The vineyard owner sends servants (the prophets) and finally his “beloved son” (Jesus). Each is rejected or killed. The parable ends with the owner’s judgement on the tenants. For Christians, this parable shows that true discipleship means recognising the Son and accepting the cost of that recognition, even when rejection and suffering follow.

The Rich Man and the Cost of Discipleship (Mark 10:17–31)

In Mark 10:17–31, a man runs up to Jesus and asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. He claims to have kept all the commandments from youth. Jesus looks at him with love and says: “One thing you lack. Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.” The man goes away sad, because he had great wealth. Jesus then says: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.”

This passage shows the cost of discipleship in concrete terms: it may require surrendering wealth, status and security. It connects to the Kingdom of God — present discipleship and future reward are linked. The disciples are astonished and ask who can be saved; Jesus replies: “With man this is impossible, but not with God; all things are possible with God.” Peter then notes that they have left everything — Jesus assures him of reward “in this present age” and in “the age to come.”

Key Fact

In Mark 10:17–31, Jesus tells the rich man to sell all his possessions, and then says “it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the Kingdom of God.” This striking image shows that discipleship may demand the surrender of everything that competes with God.

The Failure and Problems of Discipleship

Mark’s account of discipleship is unflinchingly honest about human failure. In Mark 9:14–29, the disciples who remained behind while Jesus was on the Mount of Transfiguration are unable to drive out a spirit from a boy. The father cries: “I asked your disciples to drive out the spirit, but they could not.” Jesus heals the boy and privately tells the disciples: “This kind can come out only by prayer.” Their failure is a lesson in the limits of disciples acting on their own authority without relying on God.

Most dramatically, Peter — the first and most prominent disciple — denies Jesus three times in Mark 14:66–72. A servant girl twice identifies him as a follower of Jesus; bystanders also challenge him. Each time Peter denies it, the last time with curses. The rooster crows. Peter “broke down and wept.” This is the same Peter who confidently declared “You are the Messiah.” His failure shows that discipleship is not a matter of confidence or strength but of grace. For Christians, Peter’s later restoration (implied by Mark 16:7 — the angel says “tell the disciples and Peter”) shows that failure is not the end.

In Mark 10:41–45, the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest. Jesus gathers them and says: “Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” This teaching on servant leadership defines the purpose of discipleship: not status but service, modelled on Jesus himself.

Women in the Ministry of Jesus

Mark’s Gospel gives significant attention to women as disciples, which was countercultural in the first century. In Mark 7:25–30, a Greek (Syrophoenician) woman approaches Jesus and persistently argues for her daughter’s healing. Jesus initially responds with what sounds like a rebuff, but she persists. Jesus praises her response and heals her daughter. She shows tenacity and faith in a context where Gentile women would not normally address a Jewish rabbi. Many scholars read her as a model disciple — persistent, faithful, willing to engage with rejection.

In Mark 14:3–9, an unnamed woman breaks an alabaster jar of expensive perfume and pours it over Jesus’s head. The disciples are indignant at the “waste.” Jesus defends her: “She has done a beautiful thing to me… wherever the gospel is preached throughout the world, what she has done will also be told.” Her act anticipates Jesus’s burial anointing. It is a profound act of devotion that the disciples fail to recognise.

In Mark 15:40–47 and 16:1–8, it is women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Salome — who are present at the crucifixion, witness the burial, and are the first to hear the resurrection proclamation. The male disciples have fled. This pattern of female faithfulness at the cross and tomb is significant for Christian understandings of women’s role in the Church.

Mark 8:34 contains Jesus’s definition of discipleship: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.” Three modern Christians are studied as examples of costly discipleship.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945) was a German Lutheran pastor and theologian. His book The Cost of Discipleship (1937) argued that “cheap grace” — Christianity without cost or commitment — was a heresy. Genuine discipleship required what he called “costly grace.” He put his beliefs into practice: he joined the resistance against Hitler’s Nazi regime and was arrested in 1943. He was executed at Flossünbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945, just weeks before the end of the war. His example embodies Mark 8:34 — he literally took up a cross.

Oscar Romero (1917–1980) was the Archbishop of San Salvador in El Salvador. In a deeply divided society, he became an outspoken advocate for the poor and the victims of state violence. His outspokenness made him a target. He was assassinated on 24 March 1980, shot while celebrating Mass at a hospital chapel. He was canonised by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018. His life shows discipleship as prophetic witness even at the cost of death.

Mother Teresa (1910–1997) was an Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata in 1950. She devoted her life to serving “the poorest of the poor” — the sick, the dying, and those abandoned on the streets. She connected her service explicitly to Mark 10:45 — the one who came “not to be served, but to serve.” She was canonised by Pope Francis on 4 September 2016.

Key Fact

The three modern disciples all embody Mark 8:34 (“deny themselves and take up their cross”): Bonhoeffer (German Lutheran pastor, executed 1945 for resisting Hitler), Romero (Archbishop of El Salvador, assassinated 1980 while defending the poor), Mother Teresa (Albanian-Indian nun, founded Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata 1950, canonised 2016). All three were canonised or recognised by the Church as heroes of faith.

From an atheist or Humanist perspective, religious observance such as discipleship can be seen as unnecessary. Humanists argue that compassion, service and ethical commitment do not require a religious framework — Bonhoeffer’s courage against the Nazis, or Mother Teresa’s care for the dying, reflects universal human values that anyone can hold regardless of belief. They might also question whether religious motivation can sometimes lead people in the wrong direction — history contains examples of harmful actions done in the name of following religious commands.

Christians respond that the examples of Bonhoeffer, Romero and Mother Teresa show discipleship producing exactly the kind of self-giving, justice-seeking, care-for-the-marginalised that Humanists also value — and that the explicit connection to Jesus’s teaching in Mark provides both motivation and a consistent framework for costly action that secular ethics can also affirm.
before.exam_tip_html: This is a heavy lesson — eight spec bullets. For “Outline three” questions, pick the three most specific and distinct points. For 5-mark questions, a passage reference earns the source mark: “In Mark 8:34, Jesus says ‘deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me’…” For 12-mark Discuss questions on discipleship, the non-religious alternative view must be genuinely developed: state the Humanist argument (that compassion and service don’t require religion) before offering the Christian response. Don’t just say ‘Humanists disagree’ and move on. Biographical detail on Bonhoeffer, Romero and Mother Teresa earns marks — know their dates and how each life connects to a specific Markan passage. SPaG: spell ‘Bonhoeffer’, ‘Romero’ and ‘Gethsemane’ correctly; use ‘discipleship’ as a technical term precisely.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the call of the disciples as described in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Jesus called fishermen (Simon, Andrew, James, John) beside the Sea of Galilee and they left their nets immediately to follow him (Mark 1:14-20).
• Jesus called Levi, a tax collector, with the same two words 'Follow me', and Levi got up immediately (Mark 2:13-17).
• Jesus sent the Twelve out 'two by two', instructing them to take nothing for the journey — no bread, bag or money — showing radical dependence and trust (Mark 6:7-13).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens in Mark's account of the rich man's encounter with Jesus (Mark 10:17-31).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• A man asked what he must do to inherit eternal life; Jesus told him he lacked one thing — to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow him.
• The man went away sad because he had great wealth.
• Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the Kingdom of God.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Peter's denial (Mark 14:66-72) is important for understanding discipleship.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Peter's denial shows that discipleship can fail even in those who seemed most committed — this warns Christians that discipleship requires ongoing reliance on God's grace rather than human willpower or self-confidence.
• The specific mention of Peter in Mark 16:7 ('tell the disciples and Peter') suggests that failure is not the end — Jesus offers restoration to those who have failed, giving hope to disciples who struggle.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the life of either Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Oscar Romero or Mother Teresa reflects the demands of discipleship in Mark's Gospel.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for a named source. Example using Bonhoeffer:
• Bonhoeffer's resistance to the Nazi regime reflects Mark 8:34 — 'deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me' — he quite literally risked and gave his life for his faith, demonstrating that discipleship may require sacrifice of personal safety.
• His book The Cost of Discipleship argued against 'cheap grace' — a Christianity without cost — mirroring Jesus's teaching in Mark 10:45 that the Son of Man 'came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.'
The fifth mark requires citing Mark 8:34 or Mark 10:45 as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The women in Mark's Gospel are better examples of discipleship than the male disciples.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Women are present at the crucifixion (Mark 15:40-47) when the male disciples have fled. Women are first at the tomb (Mark 16:1-8) and first to hear the resurrection proclamation. The anonymous woman who anointed Jesus (Mark 14:3-9) is praised by Jesus: 'wherever the gospel is preached... what she has done will also be told.' The Greek/Syrophoenician woman (Mark 7:25-30) persists despite apparent rejection and is praised for her faith.
Against: The male disciples were called first (Mark 1:14-20) and were sent on mission (Mark 6:7-13). Peter's confession 'You are the Messiah' (Mark 8:27-33) is a moment of genuine insight. Peter's failure (denial) is followed by restoration (Mark 16:7 — 'tell the disciples and Peter'). Judas's betrayal is the disciples' worst failure, not a representative picture. Mark's Gospel is more interested in showing the challenge of discipleship for all than in ranking disciples by gender.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:1-20) teaches about discipleship.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• The seed on the path represents those who hear the word but Satan immediately takes it away — some people do not respond at all to Jesus's call.
• The seed on rocky ground represents those who receive the word with joy but fall away when trouble or persecution comes — discipleship requires perseverance through difficulty.
• The seed in good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it and produce a large crop — true discipleship bears fruit in a changed, productive life.
